text: Before any NumPy, visualization, or quantum-SDK work in this course will run reliably, you need an isolated, reproducible Python environment, one where installing a package for this course never silently breaks some other project on your machine.

A virtual environment creates a private, self-contained copy of Python and its installed packages for a single project. venv ships with Python itself and is enough for this entire course. conda is a heavier alternative many research groups standardize on, because it can also install non-Python dependencies like compiled BLAS and LAPACK libraries. Either way, the install is the same four packages: NumPy and SciPy for computing, Matplotlib for plotting, and Jupyter for the notebook interface covered next lesson.

Creating a venv is one command, activating it is another, and once it's active, pip install only affects that isolated environment. On Windows PowerShell that's dot-backslash-venv-backslash-Scripts-backslash-Activate-dot-p-s-1. Quantum SDKs like Qiskit are intentionally not installed yet — the point of this chapter is getting the plain Python and NumPy foundation solid first.

A requirements-dot-txt file records exactly which package versions a project depends on, so the environment can be recreated identically later. Pinning exact versions with a double-equals sign matters more in scientific computing than almost anywhere else, because a different NumPy minor version can occasionally change a default behavior in a way that silently alters a numerical result — exactly the kind of bug that's hard to notice in a quantum simulation.
Next lesson reviews functions and classes through the lens of quantum simulation code, using a small Qubit class as the running example.
